description: Manually reviewed ground-truth ground-contact frame labels for the 3 real example clips (examples/my_sprint.mp4, my_sprint_2.mp4, my_sprint_3.mp4), used to validate/reject ground-contact detection approaches for contact_events.py.
methodology: Built and used scripts/label_contact_frames.py, a proper frame-scrubbing tool: for each candidate window (one per event the live detector, app.services.biomechanics.contact_events._detect_side_contacts, currently fires on for a given clip/side), it extracts every individual frame in a +/-7 frame range as its own tightly-cropped, upscaled tile (not a compressed static strip), with the tracked ankle landmark cross-marked and frame index/timestamp/normalized_y burned in, laid out as a grid. This replaces the original 4-label methodology (static image strips, 'reviewed window' terminology) that this file's own prior conclusion flagged as insufficiently rigorous. Each window below was visually reviewed frame-by-frame against this tooling. 'candidates' mode centers windows on the detector's own fired peaks (tests precision: is each fired event real?); it does not by itself surface false negatives (missed real contacts) - that would need 'uniform' mode windows, not yet reviewed at the same depth this session.

clips_reviewed.camera_description: Low, close, oblique 'lower side corner view' camera - the clip previously confirmed (via static-strip review) to show the swing-vs-stance foreshortening bug.

windows.reasoning: Foot visibly flat against the track surface across a ~5-6 frame plateau (approx f19-f24), clearly distinct from the curled-up swing posture seen in every other reviewed window on this clip. This is the first stride cycle in the clip; mechanics may differ slightly from steady-state (settling into pace), which is part of why confidence is only medium rather than high.

Across the full window the tracked foot visibly curls up and back toward the glutes (classic swing/recovery), never approaching the ground plane. The y-value peaks exactly during this curled posture - direct visual confirmation of the documented foreshortening bug, not a borderline call.
Same pattern as the f109-123 window: foot curls up behind the body through the whole window, peak y-value coincides with maximum curl, not ground contact.

Most extreme example found this session: normalized_y exceeds 1.0 at the smoothed peak (raw value 0.986, smoothed briefly >1.0), corresponding to an exaggerated swing kick with the foot held high and behind the body - unambiguously not ground contact despite being the single highest-magnitude 'contact' signal in the clip.
Foot is elevated and bent through the window; never reaches a position consistent with ground contact. Slightly less extreme curl than other false positives but still clearly swing phase.

Foot swings up and to the side through the window, no ground contact visible. Notable: this false positive's raw y (0.8971) is actually LOWER than the confirmed true contact's raw y (0.9042, f21 above) - direct evidence that no magnitude/prominence threshold on this signal can cleanly separate true contacts from false positives on this camera angle; the two classes overlap.

clips_reviewed.summary: 5 of 6 uniformly-sampled events across the full clip duration (not just 3 isolated hand-picked samples as in the original investigation) are confirmed false positives via frame-by-frame visual review - a fired event that is really swing-phase peak knee flexion. 1 of 6 is a plausible true contact. This raises the confidence of the original conclusion considerably: the false-positive rate on this camera geometry looks to be the norm across the clip, not an occasional edge case.

clips_reviewed.camera_description: Proper side-on, waist-height camera - the clip previously scored as camera_height_score: 100 and shown (via static-strip review) to perform much better (3/6 correct).

windows.reasoning: Foot progressively descends toward the ground across f57-62 (consistent with approaching contact, unlike the clear swing-curl seen on my_sprint_2), but the window is occluded by a background post/bollard for 3 frames right around the expected turnaround (f63-64, f66), and the uniform brick-paver background gives no clear ground-plane or shadow cue to confirm the exact contact frame even in unoccluded frames. Cannot assign a precise contact frame with confidence.
Entire window is occluded by a background object (a blue post/pole, likely boardwalk railing) obscuring the leg for essentially the whole window. Cannot review visually at all.

Foot visibly descends toward the ground with increasing y across f137-146 (trend consistent with approaching contact), but the window becomes occluded (same background post) for f147-151, cutting off before any plateau/turnaround is visible. Truncated - cannot confirm the actual contact frame.
Same occlusion as f106-120 - background post blocks the leg for the whole window.

clips_reviewed.summary: New finding, not previously documented: this clip has a recurring background occlusion (a post/bollard, likely a boardwalk railing) that blocks the tracked leg in 2 of 4 sampled windows, and even the unoccluded windows have a uniform brick-paver background that provides no reliable visual ground-plane cue. 'Good camera angle' (per the existing headroom/rotation quality gate) does not guarantee the footage is actually labelable - occlusion and background texture are a separate, currently unmeasured problem. No confident true/false contact label could be assigned from this clip this session.

clips_reviewed.camera_description: Archival B&W stock footage, crouching-start scene, low resolution.

windows.reasoning: This window covers the crouching sprint start / drive phase (crouched forward lean, likely just out of blocks), not steady-state running stride. The contact-detection heuristic is calibrated for the cyclical mid-stride pattern; start-phase ground contact is mechanically different (much longer, driving contact) and this heuristic was never designed or validated for it. Also, image resolution/blur makes precise visual judgment unreliable regardless.

Tracked landmark visibly jumps between the athlete's real foot position and unrelated background clutter (e.g. spectators) across the window, with several frames missing a usable landmark entirely (confidence below the 0.35 threshold). This is a tracking-reliability failure on low-resolution archival footage, not a geometric heuristic problem - the input signal itself is untrustworthy here, independent of contact_events.py's logic.
Runner's posture in this window looks upright/decelerating rather than mid-sprint-stride - likely past the finish or between takes. Same steady-state-only caveat as the f43-57 window.

clips_reviewed.summary: New finding: low-resolution archival footage introduces a confound this session hadn't isolated before - pose tracking itself becomes unreliable (landmark jumps to background clutter) at points, on top of the clip containing non-steady-state phases (start, deceleration/stop) that the heuristic was never designed for. Any future benchmark clip selection should prefer steady-state mid-run footage and should check tracking confidence, not just camera geometry, before attempting ground-contact labeling.

legacy_labels_from_prior_session.note: The following 4 labels were produced with the old static-image-strip methodology before this session's frame-scrubbing tool existed. Kept for reference/continuity, not re-verified this session.

labels.confidence: low - foot stayed low/extended for ~8 consecutive frames without a single sharp minimum, harder to pin an exact frame

conclusion: This session's frame-scrubbed review (6 uniformly-sampled events spanning the entire my_sprint_2.mp4 clip, vs. the prior 3-4 hand-picked samples) confirms the false-positive rate on a bad camera angle is high and consistent (5/6 = 83% in this sample), not an occasional edge case. It also produces a direct quantitative counterexample proving calibration cannot fix this: the one confirmed true contact (raw y=0.9042) has a LOWER magnitude than one of the confirmed false positives (raw y=0.8971) - the two classes overlap on the only signal this detector uses, so no threshold/prominence tuning on foot-height alone can separate them. Two new, previously undocumented confounds were also found: (1) 'good' camera angle per the existing quality gate does not guarantee labelable footage - my_sprint_3.mp4 had background occlusion blocking the leg in half the reviewed windows despite scoring camera_height_score: 100; (2) low-resolution archival footage can break pose-tracking reliability itself (landmark jumping to background clutter), which is a distinct problem from the geometric heuristic and would corrupt any ground-truth attempt regardless of camera angle. Recommendation for whoever picks this up next: (a) do not attempt further foot-height-based threshold tuning, the overlap evidence above rules it out; (b) if pursuing a trained classifier, it needs an input feature richer than single-signal foot height (e.g. knee+ankle+hip joint configuration, velocity, or a vision-based approach) precisely because the geometric signal itself is ambiguous between swing and stance for oblique cameras; (c) before collecting more footage for labeling, screen candidate clips for occlusion-free, steady-state, high-tracking-confidence segments first - this session lost half its my_sprint_3.mp4 windows and all of its my_sprint.mp4 windows to confounds unrelated to the core question.
